text:
I support the motion. A rule that counts the passenger as exactly one person, no more and no less, is the only impartial rule available. Bentham asks us to take everyone affected, weigh the pleasures and pains for each, and take the balance. In a crash the pains are deaths, and the balance is simple. Any rule that protects the passenger at the cost of two pedestrians chooses the worse outcome on purpose.

Think about the policy, not the single crash. A fleet programmed to minimise deaths will, across millions of journeys, kill fewer people than a fleet programmed to protect passengers. Everyone, including every future passenger, is safer living under the first rule. If the car swerves into a wall to avoid two children, one person dies instead of two. That is one family grieving instead of two.

A virtue ethicist will object that a person of good character has no number for killing an innocent passenger, and being willing to write that calculation down in advance is itself the corruption. Refusing to write the rule down does not stop the car from choosing; it only means the choice is made by accident or by marketing. Writing it down is how we take responsibility for the deaths rather than pretending nobody decided. In the end the question is which choice leaves people better off, and on that measure the answer is clear.

Bentham's principle that each counts for one and nobody for more than one settles this: the passenger cannot be weighted above the pedestrians. The feeling that it is worse to be killed by your own car is real, but it is a feeling, and it should be weighed against what is at stake. Set beside an extra death, the discomfort of the rule is small.

Bentham asks us to take everyone affected, weigh the pleasures and pains for each, and take the balance. In a crash the pains are deaths, and the balance is simple. Any rule that protects the passenger at the cost of two pedestrians chooses the worse outcome on purpose. Across a million cars, a passenger-protecting rule would cost hundreds of extra pedestrian lives a year to spare a smaller number of owners.

A Stoic will object that a rule the passenger never agreed to treats their reason as if it did not exist, so the count cannot be right while the rule is hidden. Disclosure is a good idea and costs little, so by all means publish the rule. But the rule is right because it saves more lives, and it would still be right if a particular buyer refused to read it. That is why the utilitarian answer follows the consequences, wherever they lead and whoever they favour.

Two deaths are worse than one whoever the one is, so the car should minimise total deaths even when that means sacrificing its passenger. Impartiality is the heart of the view. The passenger's life matters exactly as much as each pedestrian's, and no more. A car designed to favour its owner builds partiality into a machine that will make the same choice thousands of times across a whole fleet.

The feeling that it is worse to be killed by your own car is real, but it is a feeling, and it should be weighed against what is at stake. Set beside an extra death, the discomfort of the rule is small. We already accept that ambulances drive in ways that slightly raise their crew's risk, because more people are saved overall.

Count everyone affected, give each the same weight, and the right policy is the one with the better total.

This is basically the trolley problem, and people have argued about the trolley problem for years without agreeing. There is no right answer, so whatever the engineers pick is fine as long as they pick something. Two lives are more than one, that is just maths. I do not see why this is even a question. The car should save as many people as it can and that is the end of it.

The car should be programmed to minimise deaths, because a life saved is a life saved whether it belongs to the buyer or a stranger.

Self-driving cars will crash much less than humans do, so these cases will almost never happen. We should focus on making them safe instead of worrying about rare dilemmas that are mostly in philosophy classes. We already accept that ambulances drive in ways that slightly raise their crew's risk, because more people are saved overall.
